newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Cambodia entry in ASEAN unlikely before '98 - Siazon.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia entry in ASEAN unlikely before '98 - Siazon.

text.p: Cambodia will not become a member of ASEAN until possibly after the country's general elections in May 1998, Philippines Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Tuesday.
"I don't know. It's difficult," Siazon told Reuters when asked if a solution could be found to the Cambodian crisis and if Phnom Penh could become a member of ASEAN by its December summit.
Asked in an interview if Cambodia's membership would only be considered after a new government takes power in Phnom Penh after scheduled polls in May 1998, he said: "I think so."
Many members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) have been keen to get all 10 countries in the region into the group this year as it celebrates its 30th anniversary.
That prospect was scuttled by fighting in Phnom Penh in early July which ended with Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousting First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
ASEAN foreign ministers meeting in Kuala Lumpur last month decided to defer Cambodia's membership because of the turmoil in the country.

Diplomatic sources said ASEAN foreign ministers agreed at a special meeting on Monday in Singapore to undertake a complex mediation effort to restore stability in Cambodia, with the May 1998 general elections serving as the centrepiece of their efforts.
Their opening salvo would be to assign Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn as the main ASEAN contact for Ranariddh and Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas playing the same role with Hun Sen.

Siazon, current chairman of the ASEAN foreign ministers standing committee, said Cambodia would not have become a problem had Hun Sen waited until the country joined the group before he violently ousted Ranariddh.
"If he (Hun Sen) had only waited a few days, it would have been over," he said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia is still an observer.

ASEAN diplomats said that if Hun Sen's power grab had taken place after Cambodia had become a member, the grouping would have recognised the new government because of its policy of non-interference in the internal affairs of another country.
"But he (Hun Sen) couldn't stop the violence. It started from below," Siazon said.
He said it was very difficult to negotiate a settlement between Hun Sen, whose forces control most of Cambodia, and Ranariddh, now living abroad with many of his royalist FUNCINPEC party leaders.
"It's hard to separate them. It's been bloody. A lot of people have been killed," Siazon said.
Scores of FUNCINPEC supporters have been killed by Hun Sen forces and Ranariddh loyalists are battling desperately to hold on to their last strongholds in northwestern Cambodia.
